title: 1  In class exploration and discussion
text:
1.0.1 Exercise
Consider two generic prediction models \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) for univariate, continuous outcome \(Y \in \mathbb{R}\) with multivariate predictors \(X \in \mathbb{R}^d\). Without knowing anything about how the prediction models were created, describe how you might evaluate the performance of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) if you know the true relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\). Try to be precise in your description, using mathematical notation if helpful.

In class we discussed \(X\) as a matrix \(D\), for data, and \(Y\) as an output vector or single number \(P\), for predicitons. In between \(D\) and \(P\) there may be a \(D'\) matrix where the data is transformed. The prediction is related to some target quantity that we care about.
One way we might validate the model, is to run \(X\) through \(f\) to get \(\hat{Y}\), and then we can compare \(\hat{Y}\) to \(Y\). The specific formula from class is below: \[f: D -> D' -> P\qquad f(x_0) = {\hat{y_0}}\qquad  P \in \mathbb{R}\]
Then, we will have to consider what is the method of comparison between \(Y\) and \(\hat{Y}\)?
Some options include the following one-number summary values:



Mean Squared Error: \[\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]
Root Mean Squared Error: \[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}\]
Mean Absolute Error: \[\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i - \hat{y}_i|\]



Alternatively, we might use a visualization to evaluate this. We would plot \(Y\) vs. \(\hat{Y}\).



Calibration Curve


The plot above is the calibration curve. It is more descriptive than the available one number-summaries listed.
Q: What is the mathematical definition for “well-calibrated”? in the calibration curve? A: The expected value at \(y\) given a specific \(\hat{y}_0\) is equal to \(\hat{y}_0\). \[\mathbb{E}[y \mid \hat{y}_0] = \hat{y}_0\] OR \[\mathbb{E}[y - \hat{y}_0 \mid \hat{y}_0] = 0\] Calibration is all about the average or expectation, NOT about the spread around the line. Discrimination is another metric that looks at tightness around the line. These measures will be overly optimistic if we use the same data that built the model. More robust definitions and exploration of these concepts are continued below.



1.0.2 Exercise
Read RMS 5.1.2. Describe/define/develop an example of the following terms

Discrimination (rank based and variation based)


Rank based discrimination is an assessment of whether predicted values are ordered correctly. From RMS 5.1.2, it is a rank correlation of \(\hat{Y}\) and \(Y\), with examples including Spearman’s \(ρ\), Kendall’s \(τ\), and Somers’ \(D_{xy}\). Variation based discrimination is an assessment of whether the predicted values differ or spread across predictions. From RMS 5.1.2, it is a measure based on variation in \(\hat{Y}\), with examples including the regression sum of squares and the \(g\)–Index.


Calibration


Calibration is a measure of the average predictive accuracy for \(f\). From RMS 5.1.2, these measures assess absolute prediction accuracy. Calibration–in–the–large compares the average \(\hat{Y}\) with the average \(Y\). Calibration curves are a part of the overall calibration measures definition.


Calibration curve


This is a plots \(Y\) values (actuals) versus \(\hat{Y}\) values (predictions), which shows you the relationship between them, and can help assess performance at individual predicted values of \(\hat{y}_0\). From RMS 5.1.2, a high-resolution calibration curve or calibration–in–the–small assesses the absolute forecast accuracy of predictions at individual levels of \(\hat{Y}\). From class and as we can see below, this can help you observe calibration and discrimination.


From Claude’s assistance:  * Discrimination = “does it sort people correctly (and by how much)?”  * Calibration = “are its actual numbers trustworthy?”

Good Calibration, Bad Discrimination




This plot is clustered around the line (good calibration), but it is not spread on \(\hat{Y}\) (poor discrimination).


Sketch a calibration curve that represents good discrimination but poor calibration





Bad Calibration, Good Discrimination




This plot is spread on \(\hat{Y}\) (good discrimination) but not following the line (poor calibration).

## Function to draw the training sample for each time this needs to be run
draw_dev_sample <- function(data, sample_total = 1145, target_events = 80){
   
   ## EPV = 10 with 8 predictors requires 80 events (deaths)
   target_events <- target_events
   target_non_events <- sample_total-target_events

   ## Stratified sampling to ensure desired number of events
   # Split into events and non-events
   events_pool     <- gusto_df[gusto_df$day30 == 1, ]
   nonevents_pool  <- gusto_df[gusto_df$day30 == 0, ]

   # Draw the stratified subsample
   dev_events    <- events_pool[sample(nrow(events_pool), target_events), ]
   dev_nonevents <- nonevents_pool[sample(nrow(nonevents_pool), target_non_events), ]

   dev_sample <- rbind(dev_events, dev_nonevents)

   # Shuffle row order so events aren't grouped together
   dev_sample <- dev_sample[sample(nrow(dev_sample)), ]
}

## Function to draw the testing sample (all the rows that are not in the training sample)
draw_test_set <- function(data, dev_sample) {

library(pROC)

compute_metrics <- function(y, pred) {
  # Guard against predicted probabilities of exactly 0 or 1,
  # which would break the logit transform below
  eps <- 1e-10
  pred <- pmin(pmax(pred, eps), 1 - eps)

  # Discrimination: c-statistic (AUC)
  c_stat <- as.numeric(pROC::auc(y, pred, quiet = TRUE))

  # Calibration slope: regress outcome on the linear predictor (logit of pred)
  lp <- log(pred / (1 - pred))
  cal_fit <- glm(y ~ lp, family = binomial())
  cal_slope <- unname(coef(cal_fit)["lp"])

  # Brier score
  brier <- mean((y - pred)^2)

  c(c_stat = c_stat, cal_slope = cal_slope, brier = brier)
}
get_apparent <- function(sample_data, formula) {
  fit <- glm(formula, data = sample_data, family = binomial())
  pred <- predict(fit, type = "response")
  list(fit = fit, metrics = compute_metrics(sample_data$day30, pred))
}
eval_on_data <- function(fit, newdata) {
  pred <- predict(fit, newdata = newdata, type = "response")
  compute_metrics(newdata$day30, pred)
}
split_sample_validate <- function(sample_data, formula, train_frac = 0.6667) {
  n_train <- round(nrow(sample_data) * train_frac)
  train_idx <- sample(nrow(sample_data), n_train)

  train_set <- sample_data[train_idx, ]
  test_set  <- sample_data[-train_idx, ]

  fit <- glm(formula, data = train_set, family = binomial())
  eval_on_data(fit, test_set)
}
bootstrap_correct <- function(sample_data, formula, apparent_metrics, B = 100) {
  n <- nrow(sample_data)
  optimism_sum <- c(c_stat = 0, cal_slope = 0, brier = 0)

  for (b in 1:B) {
    boot_idx <- sample(n, n, replace = TRUE)
    boot_sample <- sample_data[boot_idx, ]

    boot_fit <- glm(formula, data = boot_sample, family = binomial())

    boot_apparent <- compute_metrics(
      boot_sample$day30,
      predict(boot_fit, type = "response")
    )
    boot_test <- compute_metrics(
      sample_data$day30,
      predict(boot_fit, newdata = sample_data, type = "response")
    )

    optimism_sum <- optimism_sum + (boot_apparent - boot_test)
  }

  avg_optimism <- optimism_sum / B
  apparent_metrics - avg_optimism
}
# This is the "outer loop body" -- one full pass of the pipeline,
# matching one box in each boxplot of Figures 1 and 2.
run_one_repetition <- function(data, formula, sample_total = 1145, target_events = 80, B = 100) {

  dev_sample <- draw_dev_sample(data, sample_total, target_events)
  test_set   <- draw_test_set(data, dev_sample)

  # Apparent performance + the fitted model (reused below)
  app <- get_apparent(dev_sample, formula)
  apparent_metrics <- app$metrics

  # Test performance: evaluate the dev_sample-fitted model on truly new patients
  test_metrics <- eval_on_data(app$fit, test_set)

  # Split-sample (50/50, matching your simplified scope)
  split_metrics <- split_sample_validate(dev_sample, formula, train_frac = 0.6667)

  # Bootstrap-corrected
  boot_metrics <- bootstrap_correct(dev_sample, formula, apparent_metrics, B = B)

  # MATH NOTE: delta = method's estimate - test performance.
  # delta = 0 means the method perfectly recovered true generalization
  # performance for this repetition. This is exactly Figure 2's y-axis.
  data.frame(
    method = rep(c("apparent", "split_sample", "bootstrap"), each = 3),
    metric = rep(c("c_stat", "cal_slope", "brier"), times = 3),
    delta  = c(
      apparent_metrics - test_metrics,
      split_metrics - test_metrics,
      boot_metrics - test_metrics
    )
  )
}
# NOTE: reduced from the paper's 500 repetitions to keep runtime
# reasonable for a live presentation. State this explicitly when
# presenting -- it's a deliberate, documented scope reduction, not
# an error.
n_reps <- 10

set.seed(17)
results_list <- vector("list", n_reps)

for (i in seq_len(n_reps)) {
  results_list[[i]] <- run_one_repetition(
    data = gusto_df,
    formula = model_formula,
    sample_total = 1145,
    target_events = 80,
    B = 100

title: 2  Week 1: Steyerberg et al. (2001)
text:
Select one of the papers from the list below


Selected Paper: Steyerberg et al. (2001) - Internal validation of predictive models: efficiency of some procedures for logistic regression analysis


For the initial exploration, do the following:

Prepare a summary of the key ideas. Be prepared to describe/illustrate the concepts in a concrete example.
Review the instructions for the student presentation and come with an idea/sketch of the simulation you’ll perform.



Key Ideas

From the opening line of the abstract: “The performance of a predictive model is overestimated when simply determined on the sample of subjects that was used to construct the model.”  The authors expand on this idea of optimism. When the model is trained and evaluated on only data within the sample, the estimated performance will be optimistic compared with the real performance on new data that is completely outside the sample. This difference is between apparent performance and test performance.
From the closing paragraph of the introduction: “In this study we compare the efficiency of internal validation procedures for predictive logistic regression models.” (also basically the title lol)  The authors walked through a comparison of the split-sample approach (test-train splits), cross-validation, and bootstrapping. Each one is an internal validation procedure that is commonly used for evaluating models.
From the opening line of section 2.4: “We evaluated several internal validation procedures that aim to test performance more accurately than is achieved by the apparent performance estimate.”  The authors set out to determine which validation procedure of those listed above is best for the logistic regression model in question. They used the GUSTO-I dataset, detailed below, and fit multiple regression models for prediction.

Dataset: GUSTO-I; n=40,830; 2,851 deaths  Working with a dataset of 30-day mortality after an acute myocardial infarction. What does that mean? They’re looking at the % of patients who die from any cause within 30 days of a heart attack.
What they want us to do: Stop doing CV and split-sample (test-train splits), and start doing regular bootstraping instead for estimation of accuracy!
How they showed it: Logistic regression was fitted in each sample with a previously specified set of eight dichotomous predictors (including shock, age>65, diabetes, etc). The apparent performance of the model fitted to the full GUSTO-I data was the reference point from which they compared the other performance measures. “The large size of the total GUSTO-I data set makes sure that the optimism in this performance estimate is negligible.” As mentioned above, they compared variants of split-sample, cross-validation, and bootstrap (including the .632 and .632+ methods) specifically at EPV=10 to analyze estimates of model performance.
Some results:

The optimism and the variability of the model performance estimates reduced as sample size increased.
“The regular bootstrap resulted in the most accurate estimates of model performance: the bias was close to zero and the variability similar to that of the apparent performance.”
Bootstrap resampling resulted in stable and nearly unbiased estimates of performance.
Relation to some other papers: “a puzzling observation was that the .632 and the .632+ bootstrap variants were not superior to the regular bootstrap.”

Definitions 

Events Per Variable (EPV): The number of outcome events (i.e. number of deaths) divided by the number of predictor variables in the model. Recommended to be at least 10 to provide an adequate predictive model. 
Internal Validation: All methods of assessing performance using only the dataset you were provided. 
External Validation: Assessing performance using a TRULY NEW dataset. Something from another clinic, a separate experiment, real world data, etc. 
Apparent Performance: Predictive performance estimated on the training sample. Optimistically biased, because the same data is used to fit and evaluate the model. 
Test Performance: Predictive performance estimated on the test data (held-out sample), an independent test set consisting of all patients from GUSTO-I except the patients in the random sample. 
Optimism: The difference between apparent performance and a model’s true performance on new data. 
Split-sample approach: Randomly split training data in two parts: one to develop the model and another to measure its performance. 
Cross-validation: Model is developed on one part of the data and tested on the other part, while these samples are randomly taken repeatedly and the average is taken as an estimate of the performance. 
Bootstrap: Replicates the process of sample generation from an underlying population by drawing samples with replacement from the original data set, of the same size as the original data set. 
Discrimination: The ability to distinguish high-risk subjects from low-risk subjects. Commonly quantified by a measure of concordance, the c statistic. 
Calibration: Whether the predicted probabilities agree with the observed probabilities. Well-calibrated models have a slope of 1, while models providing too extreme predictions have a slope less than 1. Well-calibrated models also have an intercept of 0, while models providing predictions that are too high or too low on average have an intercept different from 0.



Sketch of the simulation: Replicate a simulation from the paper
The goal is to demonstrate that the regular bootstrap returns the optimal estimates of internal validity.

Start with the GUSTO-I dataset (from R or Python package)
Generate sample and independent test sets for EPV = 10
Complete split sample and regular boostrap on the sample dataset
Compare Predictive performance (c statistic, calibration slope, Brier score, D(=scaled\(\chi^2\)), \(R^2\))

Replicating the example from the paper
The following sections replicating the simulation were assisted by Claude. I am still working to develop a full understanding of the code, formulas, and methods completed within. Formulas and comments will be added progressively.

Figures: Replicating a version of Figure 2 from the paper
In the paper, figure 2 shows bias and variability for a few of the procedures for estimating model performance in independent data for EPV = 10, including apparent performance, split-sample validation on 50% or 33% of the sample, cross-validation on 50% or 10% of the sample, and regular bootstrapping. In this simulation, I will show apparent performance, split-sample validation on 33% of the sample, and regular bootstrapping. I will also only show metrics for calibration and discrimination (c statistic, calibration slope, Brier score).

From the paper: “A logistic regression model was fitted in each sample consisting of a previously specified set of eight dichotomous predictors: shock, age>65 years, high risk (anterior infarct location or previous MI), diabetes, hypotension (systolic blood pressure <100 mmHg), tachycardia (pulse>80), relief of chest pain>1 hr, female gender”

All variables are now transformed to match the “eight dichotomous predictors” from the paper. Below, the logistic regression model is defined in R code for the upcoming simulations.



From the paper: “For example, for EPV=10 and 7.0% mortality, all training and test samples consisted of 1145 and 39,685 patients, with 80 and 2771 deaths, respectively.”



Building reusable functions for computing desired metrics:
Metric definitions
C-statistic (discrimination) — the probability that a randomly chosen patient who died is assigned a higher predicted risk than a randomly chosen patient who survived: \[c = P(\hat{p}_i > \hat{p}_j \mid Y_i = 1,\ Y_j = 0)\]


Estimated empirically as the proportion of all (event, non-event) pairs correctly ordered by the model, with ties counted as half-correct: \[\hat{c} = \frac{1}{n_1 n_0} \sum_{i:\, Y_i=1} \sum_{j:\, Y_j=0} \left[ \mathbb{1}(\hat{p}_i > \hat{p}_j) + 0.5 \cdot \mathbb{1}(\hat{p}_i = \hat{p}_j) \right]\]


where \(n_1\) is the number of events and \(n_0\) is the number of non-events. In this case from the paper, since we have a binary outcome, c is identical to the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve; c varies between 0.5 and 1.0 for sensible models (the higher the better).
Calibration slope — the coefficient \(\beta\) from an auxiliary logistic regression of the observed outcome on the linear predictor (logit of the model’s predicted probability): \[\text{logit}\big(P(Y=1)\big) = \alpha + \beta \cdot \text{linear predictor}\]


A well-calibrated model has \(\beta = 1\). \(\beta < 1\) indicates predictions that are too extreme (overfitting); \(\beta > 1\) indicates predictions that are too conservative.
Brier score — mean squared error between predicted probability and observed outcome: \[\text{Brier} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{p}_i - Y_i)^2\]


Ranges from 0 (perfect) to 0.25 (worthless) for a well-behaved binary outcome model. Exactly the same formula as MSE, but specifically used for binary prediction models.



Computing apparent performance for the logistic regression model on the training sample dataset



Defining the function to evaluate a given model on new data for the test performance



Function for the split-sample validation, essentially running a test-train split on the development sample and fitting the model.



Defining function for the regular bootstrap method. Setting B=100 as the authors did in the paper. Sampling from the sample distribution with replacement, then training on that sample. Computing performance in the following way: The performance in the bootstrap sample represents estimation of the apparent performance, and the performance in the original sample represents test performance. The difference between these performances is an estimate of the optimism in the apparent performance. This difference is averaged to obtain a stable estimate of the optimism. The optimism is subtracted from the apparent performance to estimate the internally validated performance [7]: estimated performance = apparent performance − average(bootstrap performance − test performance). In other words, we evaluate \(\text{model}_b^*\) on the bootstrap sample itself (its own “apparent” performance), and on the original sample (its “test” performance). \[\text{optimism}_b = \text{Perf}(\text{model}_b^*,\ \text{sample}_b^*) \;-\; \text{Perf}(\text{model}_b^*,\ \text{sample}_{\text{orig}})\] Average the optimism across all \(B\) replicates:


\[\overline{\text{optimism}} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} \text{optimism}_b\]


Subtract this from the apparent performance of the model fitted on the original (development) sample to get the bias-corrected estimate:


\[\text{estimated performance} = \text{apparent performance} - \overline{\text{optimism}}\]

3.1.1 Key Ideas

3.1.1.1 Stop doing X, Start doing Y!

Cross-validation is the standard way to estimate prediction error, but it’s not good enough.
Stop doing cross-validation, because the estimate of prediction error can be highly variable, even though it has low bias.
Instead, use the bootstrap method with the .632+ rule, which performs better. Bootstrap procedures are smoothed versions of cross validation, with adjustments made to correct for bias.



3.1.1.2 Key Findings

Of the 24 simulations completed, the results vary from experiment to experiment, but in terms of RMSE, the .632+ rule is an overall winner.
The improvement in reducing variability of error rate predictions in the set of simulations is roughly equivalent to a 60% increase in the size of the training set.
Bootstrap replications that give an estimate of prediction error can also be used to assess the variability of that estimate, which would be useful for inference, model selection, or comparing two models. Only studied on the leave-one-out boostrap method.



3.1.1.3 Quick reminder

What is cross validation?

Repeated evaluation with partitions of a dataset used as test-train splits to calculate an average estimate of model performance and a sense of variance in performance across folds

What is bootstrapping?

Replicates the process of sample generation from an underlying population by drawing samples with replacement from the original data set, of the same size as the original data set.
Used here for estimating variability / uncertainty of error rates

How are they different?

Normal CV partitions the data into a fixed, small number of discrete splits (k-folds), where each data point is used for testing exactly once
Leave-one-out CV trains on exactly n−1 points and tests on the 1 left-out point, repeated once per observation
Bootstrapping resamples with replacement, generating a huge number of possible “pseudo-datasets” that vary continuously in composition, rather than a handful of fixed partitions
Leave-one-out bootstrap draws many bootstrap samples with replacement and, for each observation i, averages its error only over the bootstrap samples that happened to exclude i. Each observation’s error estimate is itself an average over many different training-set compositions
How is bootstrapping a “smooth” version?

Because the bootstrap is averaged over many compositions, while the CV methods are dependent on cutoffs or possible variability in individual point predictions


Why is this better?

Smoother estimates tend to have lower variance, which is especially useful for small datasets where a handful of CV folds can each look very different from one another




3.1.1.4 How they showed it

Focused on the situation when the response is dichotomous (outcomes are 0, 1). Two of the explored prediction rules were Fisher’s linear discriminant function (LDF), and the nearest-neighbor (NN) rule. Examples of these are shown in figure 1.




Figure 1. Showing examples of LDF and NN.



Showed cross-validation as a nearly unbiased estimator of true error rate for both LDF and NN, but bootstrap-based estimator has RMSE 80% as large. Table 1 shows these simulation results.




Table 1. Showing comparison of CV and Bootstrap estimators.



While the authors only studied classification problems with 0-1 loss, they claim that the results are non parametric, so they can be applied to any prediction rule. However, regression problems may have different behavior and the statistical approach may differ.
Derived the Leave-one-out bootstrap estimator, which is a smoothed version of the leave-one-out cross-validation estimator. This is used in conjunction with the apparent error rate to create the .632 estimator, and in turn, the .632+ rule. Further explanation in the Equations section below.

\[
\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(.632+)} = \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(.632)} + \left(\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)'} - \overline{\mathrm{err}}\right) \cdot \frac{0.368 \cdot 0.632 \cdot \hat{R}'}{1 - 0.368\,\hat{R}'}
\]

Performed 24 sampling experiments, to investigate the effects of different classifiers, training set sizes, signal-to-noise ration, number of classes, and number of observations.
The results vary considerably from experiment to experiment, but in terms of RMSE, the .632+ rule is an overall winner.

3.1.3 Definitions

Cross Validation

Repeated evaluation with partitions of a dataset used as test-train splits to calculate an average estimate of model performance and a sense of variance in performance across folds

Variance

Model is too sensitive to training data, so it captures noise too. Poor prediction on unseen new data.
High variance = model is overfit
Low variance = model is more stable
\(\text{Variance} = \mathbb{E}\Big[ \big( \hat{f}(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)] \big)^2 \Big]\)

Where,
\(\hat{f}(x)\) : predicted value by the model
\(\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)]\) : average prediction over multiple training sets


Bias

Error that occurs when a model is too simple to capture the true patterns in the data.
High bias = model is underfit
Low bias = model is better fit to patterns
\(\text{Bias}^2 = \big( \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)] - f(x) \big)^2\)

Where,
\(\hat{f}(x)\) : predicted value by the model
\(f(x)\) : true value
\(\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)]\) : expected prediction over different training sets


Error Rate

Apparent Error (rate): error rate calculated when evaluating the model on the data it was trained on, typically underestimates true error (optimistic)

also referred to as training error

True Error (rate): error rate calculated when evaluating the model on new / unseen data

also referred to as generalization error

Test Error (rate): error rate calculated on a held out test set, used to estimate true error
No-Information Error (rate): error rate that would occurr if predictors had no relationship to the response

simulating what error looks like under pure guessing (section 3)
used by .632+ estimator to determine how much to trust the apparent error and bootstrap error


Relative Overfitting Rate (\(\hat{R}\))

a measure of how much a model is overfitting
scaled between 0 (no overfitting) and 1 (overfitting equal to the no-information value)

Mean Squared Error (MSE)

Average of the squared differences between predicted values and actual values

Prediction error

difference between predicted value and actual value (residual)
aggregated across many residuals using MSE, RMSE, or other statistics.

Bootstrap

Replicates the process of sample generation from an underlying population by drawing samples with replacement from the original data set, of the same size as the original data set.
used here for estimating variability / uncertainty of error rates

Point Estimate

A single value calculated from sample data used as the best guess for an unknown population parameter
Example: a computed error rate, such as apparent error, as a point estimate of the true error rate

Parametric

Fixed number of parameters estimated form the training data and used to make predictions
Examples: Linear regression, logistic regression

Nonparametric

Make few assumptions about functional form and relationships between variables
number of parameters grows with the size of the data and are flexible for modeling complex relationships
Example: k-NN, Decision Trees

0-1 loss

assignment of a 0 for a correct classification and a 1 for an incorrect classification
also called “indicator loss”

Fisher’s linear discriminant

classification method used as a prediction rule for separating data into classes or groups based on a linear boundary
smooth, because there is a single line dividing groups

Nearest neighbors

classification method used for separating data into classes or groups based on the closest points
unsmooth, because the decision boundary is local to closest points




3.1.4 Equations
Equation 8: leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of prediction error \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(cv1)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Q[y_i, r_{\mathbf{x}_{(i)}}(\mathbf{t}_i)] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Q(x_i, \mathbf{x}_{(i)})
\] where \(\mathbf{x}_{(i)}\) is the training set with the \(i\)th observation removed.
\(Q[y, r]\) is the discrepancy between a predicted value \(r\) and the actual response \(y\).
Each observation is \(x_i = (\mathbf{t}_i, y_i)\), where \(\mathbf{t}_i\) is the predictor/feature vector and \(y_i\) is the response.
\(r_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{t})\) denotes the prediction rule, fit on training set \(\mathbf{x}\), evaluated at feature vector \(\mathbf{t}\).
Equation 14: leave-one-out bootstrap estimator (smoothed version of cross-validation) \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n E_{\hat{F}_{(i)}}\{Q(x_i, \mathbf{x}^{*})\}
\] where \(\mathbf{x}^{*}\) is a bootstrap sample drawn from \(\hat{F}_{(i)}\), the empirical distribution on \(\mathbf{x}_{(i)}\).
Equation 24: The equation for the .632 estimator from Efron (1983): \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(.632)} = 0.368 \cdot \overline{\mathrm{err}} + 0.632 \cdot \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)}
\] This estimator is designed to correct upward bias in \(\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)}\) by averaging it with the downwardly biased estimate \(\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(.632)}\).
The coefficients .368 = \(e^{-1}\) and .632 were suggested by an argument based on the fact that bootstrap samples are supported on approcimately .632n of the original data points.
The new equation for the .632+ rule, introduced by this paper, puts greater weight on \(\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)}\) in situations where the amount of overfitting \(\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)} - \overline{\mathrm{err}}\) is large.
Equation 32: This equation is used in the simulation experiments of section 4. \[
\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(.632+)} = \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(.632)} + \left(\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)'} - \overline{\mathrm{err}}\right) \cdot \frac{0.368 \cdot 0.632 \cdot \hat{R}'}{1 - 0.368\,\hat{R}'}
\]
Equation 28: The relative overfitting rate \[
\hat{R} = \frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)} - \overline{\mathrm{err}}}{\hat{\gamma} - \overline{\mathrm{err}}}
\] \(\hat{R}\) ranges from 0, with no overfitting (\(\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)} = \overline{\mathrm{err}}\)), to 1, with overfitting equal to the no-information value \(\hat{\gamma} - \overline{\mathrm{err}}\).

Show leave-one-out cross-validation function
## Equation 8: leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of prediction error
## data:       the full training sample (data frame with columns y, t1, t2)
## fit_fn:     model fitting function (e.g., ldf_fit())
## predict_fn: matching predict function (e.g., ldf_predict())
##
## For each observation i: fit on all OTHER n-1 points (x_(i)),
## predict on the held-out point i, and score that one prediction.
## Averaging these n held-out losses gives Err^(cv1).
loo_cv_error <- function(data, fit_fn, predict_fn) {
  n <- nrow(data)
  losses <- numeric(n)

  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    train_data <- data[-i, ]
    test_point <- data[i, , drop = FALSE]

    fit  <- fit_fn(train_data)
    pred <- predict_fn(fit, test_point)

    losses[i] <- qloss_function(test_point$y, pred)
  }

  mean(losses)
}

Show bootstrap function
## First define bootstrap function
## Includes note to save the index of the sample data, so that the
## leave-one-out bootstrap can utilize that information
##
## NOTE: redraws if the resample happens to contain only one class --
## rare, but possible for small/imbalanced n, and LDA cannot fit
## without both classes present. This is a small, standard guard
## against a degenerate resample, not a change to the bootstrap logic.
draw_bootstrap_sample <- function(data) {
  repeat {
    idx <- sample(nrow(data), nrow(data), replace = TRUE)
    if (length(unique(data$y[idx])) > 1) break
  }
  list(sample_data = data[idx, ], included_idx = idx)
}




Show leave-one-out bootstrap function
## Equations 14-17: leave-one-out bootstrap estimate Err^(1)
## data:       the full training sample
## fit_fn:     model fitting function (e.g., ldf_fit())
## predict_fn: matching predict function (e.g., ldf_predict())
## B:          number of bootstrap replications (paper uses B = 50)
##
## For each of the B bootstrap resamples: fit on the resample, then
## predict on ALL n original points at once. For each original point i,
## keep that prediction's loss ONLY if i happened to be excluded from
## this particular resample (Equation 15's I_i^b). Averaging point i's
## kept losses over just those "excluded" replicates gives E_i
## (Equation 17); averaging E_i over all i gives Err^(1) (Equation 14).
loo_bootstrap_error <- function(data, fit_fn, predict_fn, B = 50) {
  n <- nrow(data)

  ## Running totals per original observation i:
  ##   loss_sum[i]  = sum of Q_i^b over replicates b where i was excluded
  ##   exclude_n[i] = number of replicates where i was excluded
  loss_sum  <- numeric(n)
  exclude_n <- numeric(n)

  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    boot <- draw_bootstrap_sample(data)
    fit  <- fit_fn(boot$sample_data)

    ## Predict on every original point at once -- we need Q_i^b for
    ## all i, then we'll discard the ones where i WASN'T excluded.
    preds  <- predict_fn(fit, data)
    losses <- qloss_function(data$y, preds)

    ## TRUE for observations NOT drawn into this bootstrap resample
    excluded <- !(seq_len(n) %in% boot$included_idx)

    loss_sum[excluded]  <- loss_sum[excluded] + losses[excluded]
    exclude_n[excluded] <- exclude_n[excluded] + 1
  }

  E_i <- loss_sum / exclude_n
  mean(E_i)
}

## Sanity check: leave-one-out bootstrap error for the same n = 20 sample
set.seed(17)
loo_boot_err <- loo_bootstrap_error(sample_data, ldf_fit, ldf_predict, B = 50)
cat(sprintf("Leave-one-out bootstrap error for LDF model (n = %d, B = %d): %.3f\n",

Show .632 estimator function
## Equation 24: the .632 estimator
## apparent_error: err-bar, the resubstitution/training error
## err1:           Err^(1), the leave-one-out bootstrap error
estimator_632 <- function(apparent_error, err1){
    (.368*apparent_error) + (.632*err1)
}

## Sanity check: .632 estimate for the same n = 20 sample, using the
## apparent_error and loo_boot_err already computed above
err_632 <- estimator_632(apparent_error, loo_boot_err)
cat(sprintf(".632 error for LDF model (n = %d): %.3f\n",
            nrow(sample_data), err_632))


.632 error for LDF model (n = 20): 0.413




Show .632+ estimator function, with supports
## Equations 27-32: the .632+ estimator

## Equation 27: No information error rate (gamma-hat)
## ps: observed proportion of y == 1 (p-hat-1)
## qs: observed proportion of predictions == 1 (q-hat-1)
gamma_hat <- function(ps, qs){
    (ps*(1-qs)) + ((1-ps)*qs)
}

## Equation 31: Relative overfitting rate
## NOTE: uses the raw err1 (not the truncated err1'), per the paper's definition
## NOTE: the paper describes R-hat as ranging from 0 to 1, but the raw
## formula has no upper cap -- if gamma_hat lands only slightly above
## apparent_error, the ratio can explode (confirmed via simulation: some
## replicates produced R_hat_prime in the thousands/billions). Capping
## at 1 enforces the paper's stated range and avoids a near-zero or
## negative denominator later in the .632+ formula.
R_hat_prime <- function(err1, apparent_error, gamma_hat_val){

    cond <- (err1>apparent_error) && (gamma_hat_val>apparent_error)
    raw <- ifelse(cond, (err1-apparent_error)/(gamma_hat_val-apparent_error), 0)
    #pmin(raw, 1)

}

## Equation 32: .632+ Rule used for simulations
estimator_632_plus <- function(err_632, err1, gamma_hat_val, apparent_error, r_hat_prime_val){

    ## Equation 31's truncated leave-one-out bootstrap error, Err^(1)'
    err1prime <- pmin(err1, gamma_hat_val)

    ## Calculate estimator
    numerator <- (.368*.632*r_hat_prime_val)
    denominator <- (1-(.368*r_hat_prime_val))

    err_632+((err1prime - apparent_error)*(numerator/denominator))
}


## Sanity check: .632+ estimate for the same n = 20 sample
set.seed(17)
sample_data <- generate_data(20)
ldf_model <- ldf_fit(sample_data)
preds <- ldf_predict(ldf_model, sample_data)
apparent_error <- mean(qloss_function(sample_data$y, preds))
loo_boot_err <- loo_bootstrap_error(sample_data, ldf_fit, ldf_predict, B = 50)
err_632 <- estimator_632(apparent_error, loo_boot_err)
gamhat <- gamma_hat(mean(sample_data$y), mean(preds))
rhatprime <- R_hat_prime(loo_boot_err, apparent_error, gamhat)
err_632_plus <- estimator_632_plus(err_632, loo_boot_err, gamhat, apparent_error, rhatprime)
cat(sprintf(".632+ error for LDF model (n = %d): %.3f\n",
            nrow(sample_data), err_632_plus))


.632+ error for LDF model (n = 20): 0.466




Show Monte Carlo Loop, for building Table 3
## Run every estimator once, on one freshly generated training sample.
## Returns a single ONE-ROW data frame -- one named column per estimator.
## Stacking many of these rows (one per replicate) is how "one experiment"
## becomes Table 3's Exp/SD/RMS summaries.
one_rep <- function(n, fit_fn, predict_fn, B=50, n_test=10000){

    ## All of the functions we just defined
    sample_data <- generate_data(n)
    model <- fit_fn(sample_data)
    preds <- predict_fn(model, sample_data)

    apparent_error <- mean(qloss_function(sample_data$y, preds))
    true_err <- true_error(model, predict_fn, n_test = n_test)
    cv1 <- loo_cv_error(sample_data, fit_fn, predict_fn)
    loo_boot_err <- loo_bootstrap_error(sample_data, fit_fn, predict_fn, B = B)
    err_632 <- estimator_632(apparent_error, loo_boot_err)
    gamhat <- gamma_hat(mean(sample_data$y), mean(preds))
    rhatprime <- R_hat_prime(loo_boot_err, apparent_error, gamhat)
    err_632_plus <- estimator_632_plus(err_632, loo_boot_err, gamhat, apparent_error, rhatprime)

    ## Put the results together! One row, one column per quantity.
    data.frame(
      true_err = true_err,
      apparent = apparent_error,
      cv1 = cv1,
      err1 = loo_boot_err,
      err_632 = err_632,
      err_632_plus = err_632_plus
    )
}

## Repeat one_rep() n_reps times and stack the one-row results into a
## single data frame: one row per replicate, one column per estimator.
montecarlo <- function(n_reps, n, fit_fn, predict_fn, B = 50, n_test = 10000){
  results_list <- vector("list", n_reps)

  for (r in seq_len(n_reps)) {
    results_list[[r]] <- one_rep(n, fit_fn, predict_fn, B = B, n_test = n_test)
  }

  do.call(rbind, results_list)
}

## Run the simulation for LDF, n = 20 (experiment #3), matching the

  Exp = sapply(sim_results, mean),
  SD  = sapply(sim_results, sd),
  RMS = sapply(sim_results, function(col) sqrt(mean((col - sim_results$true_err)^2)))
)

5.2 Motivating Idea for the PDP
The Partial Effects plot and Independent Conditional Expectation (ICE) plot help with visualizing a model when we don’t know the inner workings, specifically the relationships between features and outcomes. Partial Effects plots are used to investigate a single feature while holding all other features constant. ICE plots investigate a single feature while allowing the other features to vary across every individual value in the dataset. You can see how ICE plots may provide more information than the Partial Effects plot, but also provide too many lines on a given plot to be useful.
Enter the Partial Dependence Plot (PDP). We’ll take the average line across all of the ICE plot lines, to investigate the average relationship of a feature to the predicted outcome.
Partial Dependence Plot (PDP)
A partial dependence plot shows the marginal effect one or two features have on the predicted outcome of an ML model. It can show whether the relationship between target and feature is linear, monotonic, or more complex.
The partial dependence function is defined as
\[\hat{f_S}(\mathbf{x}_S) = \mathbb{E_{\mathbf{X}_C}}[\hat{f_S}(\mathbf{x}_S, X_C)]\]

\(\mathbf{x_s}\) are the features which are plotted on the x axis of the PDP. Typically only one feature is in the set \(S\). This is the feature we are investigating the effect of on the prediction.
\(X_C\) are the other features used in the machine learning model \(\hat{f}\)
If the feature vectors \(\mathbf{x_s}\) and \(\mathbf{x_C}\) are combined, they make up the total data \(\mathbf{X}\)
The partial function \(\hat{f_S}\) is estimated by calculating averages in the training data (aka. Monte Carlo): \[\hat{f_S}(\mathbf{x}_S) = (1/n) \sum^n_{i=1} \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}_S, \mathbf{x}^{(i)}_C)\]
This step is equivalent to averaging all of the ICE curves of the dataset. For each of the points along the x axis for \(\mathbf{x_s}\), you take the mean across the vertical direction (\(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_C\)).
So in this equation,

\(n\) is the number of instances in the dataset.
\(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_C\) are actual feature values from the dataset for features we are not interested in

5.3 Exploration
Let’s explore how to create and interpret the PDP.
First, we’ll generate some data from the following distribution. \[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y \mid X] &= \sqrt{5}\,\operatorname{sigmoid}(X_1 + X_3) + \sqrt{5}\,\operatorname{sigmoid}(X_2)\, X_3 \\
V[Y \mid X] &= 1 \\
\text{where} \quad & X_1, X_2 \sim N(0, 1) \\
& X_3 \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p = 0.4) \\
& \operatorname{sigmoid}(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}
\end{aligned}
\]


Show data generation function
sigmoid <- function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))

generate_data <- function(n) {
  X1 <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  X2 <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  X3 <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.4)
  mu <- sqrt(5) * sigmoid(X1 + X3) + sqrt(5) * sigmoid(X2) * X3
  Y  <- mu + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  data.frame(Y, X1, X2, X3)
}

6.0.1 Background notes

non-parametric: no coefficients are estimated, no functional form is assumed

example: KNN

hyperparameter: a tuning parameter that is set before training the model. It is NOT dependent upon the training data, and does not change during the training process. It may be tuned or adjusted outside of the training loops through grid search processes, but that requires training many individual models according to the hyperparameter selections

example: \(k\) in KNN

*parameter: a parameter that is learned during the model training, based on the training data

example: \(\beta\) in regression

standardization: (also called feature scaling, and also helpfully also called Z-score normalization) rescales data so that every feature has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. This is especially helpful for KNN, because magnitude of features has a significant effect on the model.
curse of dimensionality: as the dimension increases, meaning the number of features used for prediction grows, the nearness of training data to a new points decreases, because things are just further away in high dimensional space. Therefore, KNN works well in low dimensions, but not so well in high dimensions.



6.0.2 K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)

Given a new observation, return the average outcome value based on the \(k\) nearest values in the training set.

“Nearest” or closeness is determined by a distance function, most commonly the Euclidean distance.

This model is non-parametric, because no coefficients are estimated and no functional form is assumed
\(k\) is the hyperparameter determining how many points should be included in the predicted outcome for a new point provided to the model

if \(k\) is small, there are few local points used to make the prediction
as \(k\) grows, more local to global points are used in the prediction average
increasing \(k\) makes the model more smooth and trades variance for bias (lower variance, higher bias)

Standard KNN workflow:

standardize the predictors
fit on the training data
generate predictions on a grid
plot a partial effect plot for one predictor


Key Callout - “The bias-variance tradeoff. At \(k=1\), KNN memorizes the training data — zero bias on training observations, high variance across different training sets. At \(k=n\), it ignores everything except the mean — high bias, low variance. The optimal \(k\) sits somewhere in between, and finding it requires the cross-validation tools from Module 3. This tradeoff — and the challenge of navigating it — is the central tension in all of predictive modeling.”


6.0.3 Random Forests

Built on the decision tree

continually splitting the predictor space into partitions through binary splits
at each step, determine the splita cross the space that reduces within-node MSE
REPEAT until a termination condition is met
also called “recursive binary partitioning”

dendrogram: the branching diagram that gives decision trees their name, and also the way to visualize the splits made in the decision tree
“The random forest averages many trees, each trained on a different bootstrap sample of the training data. Averaging over many unstable but roughly unbiased models reduces variance without increasing bias — the central maneuver behind ensemble methods.”

Because each tree is different when different bootstrap samples are used, we want to average over them to get the “best” model.

The “random” in random forests is from the feature randomization that happens at each split. For every split, you only get to choose from a subset of the overall features, so that not every tree ends up being dominated by the same feature splits. Typically you use \(p/3\) at each step to determine the number of features available.

This reduces correlation among the trees so we have a model with lower variance.

Key hyperparameters:

\(B\): the number of trees

more stable predictions, more reliable error estimate
more computation required

\(mtry\): the number of predictors considered at each split

smaller mtry leads to less correlation between trees
larger mtry leads to less feature randomization





6.0.4 Neural Networks
From Tom’s content: “it constructs a prediction surface from the predictors using a particular functional form, which is often called a network.”
What does that mean? It is a continuous prediction surface that is smooth, not rectangular or stair-step like you would see in K-Nearest Neighbors or Random Forests. All points in the training set contribute to all weights in the network, so information sharing is global.
Neuron: basic building block of a neural network - receives linear combination of inputs, passes result through a non-linear function, produces a single number Layers: arrangement of neurons - first layer receives predictors \((x_1, x_2, ..., x_p)\) - hidden layers transform the output of a previous layer into a new representation - final layer produces the prediction \(\hat{y}\)
In the diagram 5.21, x1 and x2 are the individual neurons receiving predictors, the first layer. It passes through no hidden layers, so the predictors are directly related to the prediction \(\hat{y}\). There are weights on the lines connecting the neurons, which we can consider the betas in a linear regression. Therefore, this representaiton is equivalent to a linear regression.
We need nonlinear activation functions in the hidden layers, because otherwise we’d just be modeling linear relationships, since our network is just doing multiplication and addition throughout the layers. - From Tom: “Without nonlinear activation, the forward pass simplifies to … linear regression. Every additional hidden layer without activation collapses in the same way. The nonlinear activation is the essential ingredient.”

7.0.1 Motivating ideas and chronology
Our brains are incredible recognition and prediction machines. How do they work? Can we replicate the behavior artificially in a computer?
The provided papers give an chronology of the ideas in published literature.

Turning neuroscience into calculus.

7.0.2.2 Some equations
Let’s start with the example for the single hidden layer. The full equation for going from input \(\mathbf{x}\) to predicted \(\hat{y}\) is
\[
\hat{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}_{\text{out}}^t \,

\]
This is also called the “forward pass”, to go from input \(\mathbf{x}\) to a prediction \(\hat{y}\).

\(W_1\) is the \(m \times p\) weight matrix for the hidden layer, given a network with \(p\) predictors and \(m\) hidden neurons.
\(\mathbf{b}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^m\) is the hidden layer’s bias vector
\(\sigma(\cdot)\) is a nonlinear activation function applied element-wise
The hidden layer’s outputs are then combined linearly using the output-layer weights \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{out}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) and bias \(b_{\text{out}} \in \mathbb{R}\).
In Figure 7.2 there are \(p = 2\) inputs and \(m = 4\) hidden neurons, so \(W_1\) is a \(4 \times 2\) matrix, \(\mathbf{b}_1\) and \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{out}}\) each have 4 entries, and each arrow in the figure is one weight.

7.0.2.4 Training the model
The network is trained by minimizing a loss function over the training data. For a continuous outcome, the loss is mean squared error:
\[
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \bigl(y_i - \hat{y}(\mathbf{x}_i)\bigr)^2
\]
We minimize the loss function through gradient descent, where the weights are updated iteratively in the direction that reduces the loss most steeply. At each step,
\[
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta \, \nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}
\]
\(\eta > 0\) is the learning rate, which controls the size of each step. If it is too large, the optimizer diverges; if it is too small, convergence is slow. Other key training hyperparameters are the number of epochs (passes over the training data) and the batch size (how many observations are used to estimate each gradient update).
The gradients \(\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}\) are computed efficiently by applying the chain rule backwards through the network, from the output layer to the first hidden layer. This procedure is called backpropagation.

7.0.3.0.2 Training settings
Using scikit-learn’s MLPRegressor (multi-layer perceptron) to set up the network definition function. In subsequent tests, we will only change the hidden layers argument.


Code
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error

def make_network(hidden_layers, seed=1717):
    return MLPRegressor(
        hidden_layer_sizes=hidden_layers,  # neurons in each hidden layer
        activation="relu",                 # sigma(z) = max(0, z)
        solver="sgd",                      # (stochastic) gradient descent
        learning_rate_init=0.01,           # eta, the learning rate
        max_iter=100,                      # maximum number of epochs
        batch_size=64,                     # observations per gradient update
        alpha=0,                           # no penalty, so the loss is just MSE
        random_state=seed,                 # which random starting weights to use
    )

def predict_minutes(model, X_s):
    # the network predicts standardized y, so convert back to minutes
    y_s = model.predict(X_s)
    return y_scaler.inverse_transform(y_s.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()

title: 10  Explainer
text:
10.1 The Linear Model
Let’s go to where it all starts for many of us, y = mx+b.
This is probably what initially pops into most people’s head when they think of a linear model.
We put in some value for x that we are given or observe, then multiply that by a value of m, which we commonly call the slope, and then we add an intercept term, b, in order to get our output value of y.
If we repeatedly do this, we can get a bunch of values of y, and we could plot a general line for this relationship between x and y, or inputs and outputs.
This y=mx+b is a model, with the parameters of m and b. In the following discussion, we will talk about what it means to use different parameters for our models with the same inputs and outputs along with a slightly different and much expanded idea of a linear model than the one our teachers illustrated in school.
The linear model that we are exploring here is the linear regression model with the following components. Y is the scalar outcome, and x is a vector of predictor values for that outcome.
It has a conditional mean component, which can be expressed as \[E[Y \mid \mathbf{x}] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p
  = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^p x_j \beta_j
  = \sum_{j=0}^p x_j \beta_j
  = \mathbf{x}'\mathbf{\beta}\] where we set x0=1 to absorb the intercept into the dot product.
It also has a conditional variance component \[\text{Var}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma^2\]
Which leads to the following conditional distribution \[Y \mid \mathbf{x} \sim \text{Normal}(\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{\beta},\; \sigma^2)\]
Now in contrast to the super simple model we started with and then this scalar model we outlined above, we typically work with n observations simultaneously, so it is better for us to work with matrix notation instead. We let Y be the nx1 vector of outcomes and X be the nx(p+1) design matrix.
Now our notation for the model is \[Y = X\beta + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \text{Normal}(\mathbf{0}_n,\; \sigma^2 I_n)\]
Y is an nx1 vector of outcomes, where Yi is the outcome for observation i X is the nx(p+1) design matrix, where the first column is all ones for the intercept; Xij is the j-th predictor value for observation i B is the p+1 x 1 coefficient vector, B0 is the intercept, Bj is the coefficient for the j-th predictor sigma^2 is a scalar for the conditional variance epsilon is an nx1 error vector 0n is a vector of all zeroes of length n In is the identity matrix of size n
In the scalar form, you might write \[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \varepsilon_i,
\qquad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Normal}(0,\, \sigma^2)\]
We have four important assumptions to track here 1. Linearity in parameters: E[Y|x] is linear in B. 2. Independence of errors: epsilon_i are independent across observations 3. Homoscedasticity: Var(epsilon_i) = sigma^2 for all i 4. Normality of errors; epsilon_i are normally distributed with mean 0 and variance sigma^2

title: 10  Explainer
text:
10.2 Nonlinearity
We just worked through how we might approach a model if the relationship between our input and output were linear. However, we can think of plenty of situations where the relationship we’re trying to model is not linear.
The question then is, can we apply the model we’ve outlined in some way to model this other relationship? And lucky for us the answer is yes.
We get to do some math that changes how we set the parameters for our model, so that we can model the nonlinear relationship. The general idea of how we do this is called basis expansion.
One key note to point out is that the linear model means that we have linearity in the parameters, not necessarily the predictors. In the examples below, we have a linear relationship in B in both equations, but a non linear relationship with x in the second equation. However, if we were to treat x and x^2 as two separate predictors, then the model is a standard linear model wiht two columns in X, the design matrix.
That idea of treating things as separate predictors and replacing it with a set of derived features is called basis expansion.

10.2.1 Basis expansion
The generalized formula for basis expansion is below, \[E[Y \mid x] = \beta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \beta_k \, b_k(x)\] where \([b_0(x), \ldots, b_K(x)]\) represent the set of derived features or basis expansion of predictor x. These are chosen so that a linear combination of these can approximate nonlinear functions of x. The model is still linear in the beta parameters, so we can still solve the normal equations.
In the following sections, we will get an overview of different types of basis expansion models. First, let’s generate and load in some data to work with.

n_selected <- sum(coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.1se") != 0) - 1  # subtract intercept
c(`Non-zero gene expression features of 4,088 at lambda.1se` = n_selected)

Non-zero gene expression features of 4,088 at lambda.1se 
                                                      24 


This selection of \(\lambda\) keeps only a small fraction of the features we had originally. We are now working with just 24 features of the original 4,088.

fit_lasso <- glmnet(riboflavin$x, riboflavin$y, alpha = 1)
plot(fit_lasso, xvar = "lambda", label = FALSE,
     main = "Lasso path: -log(λ)")








Answer:
Finally, we see the coefficient path for Lasso with our selected \(\lambda\). Note that Lasso does perform variable selection, so all coefficients are equal to zero initially, and they are introduced to the model as \(\lambda\) is reduced (moving to the right on our graph).


11.1.8 Problem 5: Elastic Net
Fit an elastic net with \(\alpha \in \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}\). For each \(\alpha\), record the minimum CV-MSE. Create a small table showing \((\alpha,\, \lambda_{\min},\, \text{min CV-MSE})\). Which \(\alpha\) yields the lowest CV-MSE? How does the number of selected features compare to lasso?

set.seed(17)

cv_results <- lapply(alphas, function(a) {
  set.seed(17)
  cv <- cv.glmnet(riboflavin$x, riboflavin$y, alpha = a, nfolds = 10)
  n_selected <- sum(coef(cv, s = "lambda.min") != 0) - 1  # subtract intercept
  list(alpha = a, lambda.min = cv$lambda.min, cvm.min = min(cv$cvm), features = n_selected)
})

result_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cv_results, function(r)
  data.frame(alpha = r$alpha,
             lambda.min = round(r$lambda.min, 4),
             min_CV_MSE = round(r$cvm.min, 4),
             num_features = r$features)))
print(result_df)

2  0.50     0.0837     0.2488           55

Answer:
We see in the table above that the \(\alpha\) value of 0.75 produces the lowest CV-MSE. We also see that the number of selected features decreases as \(\alpha\) increases. That’s the expected behavior, because a value of \(\alpha = 1\) would be pure lasso, and we would expect a model with fewer features as above.


11.1.9 Problem 6: PCR
Fit PCR using the pls package (or manual SVD as shown in the chapter). Select the number of components \(k\) via cross-validation (use validationplot). Report the optimal \(k\).

               main = "PCR: CV MSE vs. number of components")







# Identify optimal k

Optimal number of components.24 comps

Answer:
The optimal \(k\) is shown above.

Back-transform the PCR fit to obtain the full 4,088-dimensional coefficient vector \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{PCR}}\).


Use \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{PCR}}\) to generate a prediction for the first observation in the dataset (X[1, ]). Show your R code and the predicted value.

Answer:

In one sentence, explain why you needed all 4,088 gene expression values to generate this prediction even though you only fit \(k\) principal components.

Answer:
We need all 4,088 gene expression values to generate this prediction because each of the \(k\) principal components is a linear combination of all of the features. PCR is not a data reduction technique, it just reduces the complexity of the model, not the dimensionality of the data required for prediction.


11.1.10 Problem 7: Comparison
Comparing across methods:

Report the CV-MSE at the selected tuning parameter for each of the four methods (ridge, lasso, elastic net, PCR).

Answer:

Answer:

Answer:
I expect that ridge would reduce the CV-MSE further than lasso, but the lasso will provide a more interpretable and smaller model in terms of the number of predictors retained. I think the CV-MSE will be further reduced when you keep all the coefficients from ridge, but lasso will ultimately be a better approach for us.

title: 12  Paper: Lasso’s Victory Lap
text:
12.1 1. Sparsity
Paper: Tibshirani, R. (2011). “Regression shrinkage and selection via the lasso: a retrospective.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology), 73(3), 273–282. link
A victory lap, reflection, and some additional ideas about the original Lasso Paper 1996.
Key points to highlight: 1. Sparsity - And the extended applications from the table 2. L1 and Convex idea - contrast with Ridge 3. Why do you do relaxed lasso? - ‘S’ stands for screening, not selection! 4. Critiques - Bayesian - Correlated Predictors 5. Response - Known gap is inference
A model is sparse when most of its coefficients are exactly zero. Write the active set as \(S = \{j : \beta_j \ne 0\}\) with size \(s = |S|\). Sparsity means \(s \ll p\): only a few predictors actually matter.
The lasso is least squares with an \(\ell_1\) penalty (details in Section 2), and its defining feature is that it returns sparse solutions. It sets some coefficients exactly to zero, so shrinkage and variable selection happen in one step. For a single standardized predictor whose least-squares coefficient is \(z\), the lasso estimate is
\[
\hat\beta = \text{sign}(z)\,(|z| - \lambda)_+ ,
\]
so any coefficient with \(|z| \le \lambda\) is set to 0, not just made small.
Why sparsity matters. One of Tibshirani’s explanations for the slow uptake of the 1996 paper is that “the statistical and numerical advantages of sparsity were not immediately apparent.” Those advantages are:

title: 12  Paper: Lasso’s Victory Lap
text:
Statistical: a sparse model is easier to interpret (you can name the predictors that matter) and estimates fewer parameters, so it has lower variance. Sparsity is also what makes \(p \gg n\) workable. Bühlmann’s discussion shows the lasso’s prediction error grows only like \(\sqrt{\log p / n}\) when the true \(\beta\) is sparse.
Numerical: algorithms can exploit sparsity. In coordinate descent, a coefficient that is 0 and stays 0 costs almost nothing to update (see the Computation notes below).


12.1.1 Extended applications (Table 1)
The paper’s Table 1 shows that the \(\ell_1\) idea carries over to other problems. Each method below puts an \(\ell_1\)-type penalty on a different object, so a different thing becomes sparse:

title: 12  Paper: Lasso’s Victory Lap
section: 12.2 2. The \(\ell_1\) penalty, convexity, and the contrast with ridge
text:
12.2 2. The \(\ell_1\) penalty, convexity, and the contrast with ridge
Assume standardized predictors \(x_{ij}\) and a centered response \(y_i\), for \(i = 1, \ldots, N\) and \(j = 1, \ldots, p\). The lasso solves
\[
\hat\beta^{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_{\beta} \; \sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big(y_i - \sum_{j=1}^{p} x_{ij}\beta_j\Big)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j|.
\]
The same problem can be written as a constraint:
\[
\min_\beta \sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big(y_i - \sum_j x_{ij}\beta_j\Big)^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_j |\beta_j| \le t .
\]
Each \(\lambda\) matches some budget \(t\).
Contrast with ridge. Ridge regression has the same form with a squared (\(\ell_2\)) penalty, \(\lambda\sum_j \beta_j^2\), or equivalently the constraint \(\sum_j \beta_j^2 \le t\). That one change in the penalty changes the behavior:









Ridge (\(\ell_2\))
Lasso (\(\ell_1\))




Penalty
\(\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2\)
\(\lambda\sum_j\lvert\beta_j\rvert\)

yes: \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\)
no (needs an algorithm; see Computation notes)

yes

no, only shrinks

Bridge family and convexity. Tibshirani puts both methods into the bridge family of penalties \(\sum_j |\beta_j|^q\):










\(q\)

Key point: \(q = 1\) is the smallest value of \(q\), so the one closest to subset selection, that still gives a convex problem. Convexity is what makes the lasso cheap to compute: any local minimum is the global minimum, and fast algorithms are guaranteed to find it. Best subset is the “ideal” selector, but it is a combinatorial search over \(2^p\) models. The lasso is the closest you can get to it while keeping the problem convex.
The figure below shows why the corners matter. The constraint regions \(\sum_j |\beta_j|^q \le 1\) have corners on the axes only when \(q \le 1\). A corner on an axis is a point where one coefficient is exactly zero. The RSS contours usually touch the lasso diamond first at a corner, which is where sparsity comes from. They touch the smooth ridge circle at a point where both coefficients are nonzero.


Code
theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 800)
lq_ball <- function(q) {
  # points on the boundary of |b1|^q + |b2|^q = 1
  r <- (abs(cos(theta))^q + abs(sin(theta))^q)^(-1 / q)
  cbind(r * cos(theta), r * sin(theta))
}
qs   <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 4)
cols <- c("grey50", "firebrick", "steelblue", "darkgreen")
